name: open-design
intent: Build the protection mechanism out of public, independently reviewable primitives and rest the system's security on the secrecy of keys or credentials alone, so that publishing the design, shipping code to untrusted hosts or having it reverse-engineered cannot defeat the protection.
problem: Protection that quietly depends on the design staying hidden: a proprietary "encryption" scheme, an obfuscated client, a hidden endpoint or parameter, a credential compiled into the artifact, an algorithm padded with secret constants. The trigger is structural: parts of the system must be published or distributed (open-source products, protocols that must interoperate, client and mobile code that runs on machines the attacker controls, standards and audits), and the design is recoverable anyway - decompilers, memory dumps, debuggers and captured devices make "nobody will figure this out" a schedule rather than a property. Teams that rely on obscurity discover only after disclosure that the protection was the secrecy, and by then it cannot be rotated because it is baked into the design.
context: Applies wherever a protection mechanism must survive scrutiny and distribution: cryptographic or protocol design, client-side and on-device code, open-source and interoperable products, published standards, and any design whose threat model includes a motivated attacker holding a copy of the artifact (Kerckhoffs 1883; Shannon's "the enemy knows the system"). It also applies as a design-review rule: any mechanism whose strength would fall if its inner workings appeared in a blog post, a leak, a debugger session or a competitor's reimplementation should be redesigned so that only key material and other cheaply replaceable secrets need to stay private.
benefits: Disclosure stops being a compromise: the mechanism can be published, shipped to untrusted clients and studied by attackers without losing its protective value, because its strength rests on key secrecy rather than design secrecy.

Review scales: a mechanism that may be published can be examined by many independent reviewers - standards bodies, auditors, open-source users, cryptanalysts - and each review no longer risks compromising the safeguard it assesses (Saltzer & Schroeder's argument for decoupling mechanism from key).

The secret becomes small and cheap to change: rotating a key is an operational step, while redesigning a scheme whose secrecy leaked is a product-wide migration; Kerckhoffs's principle points out that the things kept secret should be those least costly to change if disclosed.

Interoperability and compliance come with it: published algorithms and protocols (AES-GCM, ChaCha20-Poly1305, RSA-OAEP, Ed25519, TLS, HKDF) are what other parties, standards and certifications require, and vetted implementations with public test vectors can be verified by anyone.

Security becomes testable and arguable: you can point at a published primitive and its cryptanalysis record, run known-answer tests, and report failures without first dismantling a wall of secrecy - instead of asserting that a private scheme is unbreakable.

It forces the real secret to be treated as such: once the design may be public, key generation, distribution, storage, rotation and destruction become the named critical path rather than an afterthought of the implementation.
tradeoffs: Publication invites attack and requires a response process: the mechanism can be studied, fuzzed and attacked by everyone, and its weaknesses become public findings with disclosure timelines and coordinated-fix obligations instead of private to-dos.

Open design does not implement or audit itself: a public primitive can still be misused - reused nonces, ECB mode, fixed IVs, homegrown compositions - so the rule buys nothing without the key-management and misuse-resistance work that goes with it (the Web Crypto API and libsodium documentation are warnings about exactly this hazard).

All security pressure moves onto key management: if the design is public, the keys are the whole secret, so generation, distribution, rotation, revocation, backup and hardware protection become mandatory operational capabilities - and one key-management failure is a total failure rather than a partial one.

Standard primitives bring dependency, version and compliance constraints: you inherit the library's release cadence, its export and FIPS questions and its algorithm policy, and you lose the freedom to tune or quickly swap the mechanism that a private design (for better or worse) seemed to have.

There is a bounded, legitimate role for obscurity, and it is easy to confuse the roles: hidden details can raise an attacker's cost as defense in depth (CWE-656 allows obscurity as "one small part of defense in depth"), but treating them as the primary control is what turns obscurity into the vulnerability.

Legacy and interoperability can pin weak-but-public algorithms: a published design that shipped once is expensive to migrate, so compatibility keeps obsolete choices alive unless algorithm agility - negotiation, versioned keys, crypto-periods - is planned from the start.

participants.responsibility: The published, reviewable scheme - algorithm, protocol, key derivation or access rule - whose strength does not depend on hiding how it works; it is expected to be inspected, standardised and reimplemented by others.

The small, replaceable element - key, password, token, seed - whose secrecy is the only thing the design relies on, and which therefore carries all of the generation, storage, rotation and destruction obligations.

Whoever publishes and subjects the mechanism to scrutiny: standards body, auditor, open-source maintainer, cryptanalyst or the skeptical user Saltzer & Schroeder describe; their access to the mechanism must not compromise it.

The threat model itself: an attacker with a copy of the design, the binary or the device, who may reverse-engineer, debug and reason about the mechanism - and whose success must depend on breaking or stealing the key, not on learning the design.
The runtime role that holds, distributes and rotates the secrets - KMS, HSM, keystore, secret manager, credential rotation practice - since the pattern moves every defence onto this path.

use_cases: Cryptography and protocols: use standard, published algorithms and modes (AES-GCM, ChaCha20-Poly1305, RSA-OAEP, Ed25519, HKDF) and published protocols (TLS), keeping only keys private - the Kerckhoffs/Shannon formulation; never a private cipher or a "customized" composition.

Client-side and on-device code: mobile apps, desktop binaries and browser JavaScript run on the attacker's machine, so the design is readable by construction; protection must rely on keys and server-side enforcement, not on hidden client logic (client-side authentication is CWE-656's own example).

Open-source and widely distributed products: when the source is published or the artifact is mirrored, the design is already public; the review the community performs must not also be the vulnerability - hash passwords with published schemes, verify signatures, use standard KDFs and crypto libraries.

Published standards, interoperability and procurement: systems that must talk to third parties or be certified need openly specified mechanisms and documented key handling; a secret scheme cannot be implemented independently by another vendor or evaluated by an auditor.

Embedded and hardware products: devices reach attackers' benches, firmware is extracted and chips are decapped; the algorithm can be public while keys are protected by hardware - TEE, Secure Element/StrongBox, Secure Enclave, HSM.

Design review of existing systems: audit for "the security is the secrecy" - hardcoded keys or passwords in binaries and scripts, hidden-but-unprotected admin endpoints, obfuscation as the only barrier, secret URL schemes or parameter names used as access control - and replace the secrecy with a keyed, public mechanism.

Signal Protocol: Signal publishes X3DH, Double Ratchet and related specifications while deployments keep identity and session keys as key material; readers can inspect the protocol mechanics without relying on hidden algorithms.

OpenSSH: SSH protocol specifications and public-key authentication are documented openly; authorization depends on private keys and server-side key policy, not secrecy of the wire protocol or implementation.

TLS 1.3: IETF RFC 8446 openly specifies the handshake, record protection and key schedule so independent stacks interoperate; security rests on negotiated cryptographic keys and authenticated credentials, not a secret protocol design.
avoid_when: There is no secrecy-dependent protection at all - the mechanism is public by nature (a checksum, a rate limit, a public directory): the rule has nothing to fix, and the review should look instead at fail-safe defaults and complete mediation.

The system is a throwaway prototype with one trusted caller and no distribution: use the standard primitive anyway (there is no cheaper correct option), but skip the publication and review apparatus - a fixed, documented library call is the simple answer.

Obscurity is being used as additional depth on top of a keyed public mechanism (stripped symbols, random endpoint names, log scrubbing): that is legitimate and cheap, so keep it - the rule only forbids letting it carry the security.

Regulatory or contractual constraints genuinely require the implementation to stay confidential (classified designs, export-controlled hardware): the design can still be based on published primitives and open to qualified reviewers; if even that is impossible, treat the exception as an explicit, documented risk rather than as normal practice.
anti_patterns: "Security through obscurity" as the control: a private algorithm, an obfuscated client, a hidden endpoint or a secret header value carrying the protection, so disclosure - a decompiler, a leak, a debugger, a captured device - silently removes it.

Hardcoded or shipped secrets: keys, passwords, API tokens or seeds compiled in, echoed in logs or baked into images (the classic client-side credential), the practical form of a design whose secret sits in the wrong place (CWE-656 precedes CWE-321 and CWE-259).

"Custom crypto" as a differentiator: a homegrown cipher, a "hardened" mode, a novel composition of standard parts that has never been analysed - published or not, it forfeits the review the principle exists to buy.

Mythical secrecy of the deployed artifact: "nobody can decompile our app", "the JavaScript is minified", "customers cannot read the firmware" - assumptions of protection from inaccessibility that reverse engineering routinely disproves.
Zombie secrets: keys that cannot be rotated because they are hardcoded, burned into a protocol or part of the design, forcing a redesign when disclosure happens instead of a key rotation.
design_principles: Open design (Saltzer & Schroeder, 1975, design principle d): the design should not be secret; mechanisms should depend on "the possession of specific, more easily protected, keys or passwords", which permits examination by many reviewers without compromising the safeguards.

Kerckhoffs's principle / Shannon's maxim: a cryptosystem must remain secure when everything about it except the key is public knowledge; "the enemy knows the system" is the assumption under which the design must be evaluated.
Separation of mechanism and secret: strength lives in the key, not in the code; the mechanism may be examined, published and reused without weakening the protection.
Economy of secrets: the fewer and simpler the secrets that must be kept, the easier they are to protect - every additional secret creates another failure point and cannot be reviewed away.

Complete mediation: publication of the mechanism is only safe when it is also enforced - the keyed check must cover every access, or the openness of the design merely advertises an unbypassable-looking hole.
best_practices: Choose published, vetted primitives and standard constructions: AES-GCM or ChaCha20-Poly1305 for symmetric AEAD, X25519/Ed25519 or RSA-OAEP for asymmetric, HKDF/PBKDF2/Argon2 for derivation, TLS for transport - from the platform or the dominant audited library, with published test vectors.

Keep every secret out of the design and out of the artifact: no keys, passwords, tokens, seeds or fixed IVs in source, images, firmware, client bundles or shipped configuration; fetch them from a keystore, KMS or secret manager, scope them per environment and rotate them on a schedule.

Write the threat model down with a know-the-system attacker: state what an attacker may read (everything), what must stay secret (key material, and perhaps business data), and re-ask "what does disclosing this cost us?" for every mechanism, default, endpoint and error message.

Review before you publish or ship: treat open sourcing, a client release, a firmware flash or a protocol specification as a security-review trigger - remove embedded secrets, strip debug surfaces, and confirm each mechanism is either public-and-sound or properly keyed.
Plan agility: version key material and mechanisms so that a published weakness (a deprecated mode, an algorithm retirement) can be migrated by re-keying rather than by redesigning the product.

Use obscurity only as depth: stripping symbols, randomizing endpoints, obfuscating clients and scrubbing logs may raise attacker cost, but design as though all of it is absent (CWE-656's allowed role).
sources: Saltzer & Schroeder, "The Protection of Information in Computer Systems", Proceedings of the IEEE 63(9), 1975 - design principle (d) open design: "The design should not be secret. The mechanisms should not depend on the ignorance of potential attackers, but rather on the possession of specific, more easily protected, keys or passwords."

Kerckhoffs, La cryptographie militaire, Journal des sciences militaires, 1883 - the principle that a cryptosystem should be secure even if everything about it except the key is public knowledge, phrased by Shannon as "the enemy knows the system" (Shannon's maxim).

Schumacher, Fernandez-Buglioni, Hybertson, Buschmann & Sommerlad, Security Patterns: Integrating Security and Systems Engineering, Wiley 2006 - the security-patterns canon referenced by this catalog's Section 8, whose Security design rules group owns this row.

OWASP Developer Guide, Principles of security (Open Design): "The open design security principle states that the implementation details of the design should be independent of the design itself, allowing the design to remain open while the implementation can be kept secret. This is in contrast to security by obscurity where the security of the software is dependent upon the obscuring of the design itself."

CWE-656: Reliance on Security Through Obscurity - "Always consider whether knowledge of your code or design is sufficient to break it" and "When available, use publicly-vetted algorithms and procedures, as these are more likely to undergo more extensive security analysis and testing."
